::: {#exm-discrete-prior}
#### A discrete prior on a grid: 8 successes in 10 trials

Suppose $\prob$ can take only the eleven values $0, 0.1, 0.2, \ldots, 1$,
and we give them equal prior probability, $\p(\prob) = 1/11$.
We observe $x = 8$ successes in $n = 10$ independent trials,
so that given $\prob$ the count is $\operatorname{Binomial}(10, \prob)$:

$$
\p(x \mid \prob) = \binom{10}{x}\prob^{x}(1-\prob)^{10-x}.
$$

Because $\prob$ is discrete,
the [marginal likelihood](#def-marginal-likelihood) is a sum over the grid
rather than an integral,
and @thm-bayes-posterior gives

$$
\p(\prob \mid x = 8)
= \frac{\p(x = 8 \mid \prob)\, \p(\prob)}
{\sum_{\prob'} \p(x = 8 \mid \prob')\, \p(\prob')},
$$

where the sum runs over the eleven grid values $\prob'$.
The table builds the posterior one column at a time:
the prior, the likelihood of the observed count,
their product, and the product divided by its sum.

```{r}
#| label: discrete-prior-table
#| code-fold: false
n_trials <- 10
x_obs <- 8

discrete_post <- data.frame(prob = seq(0, 1, by = 0.1))
discrete_post$prior <- 1 / nrow(discrete_post)
discrete_post$likelihood <- stats::dbinom(
  x_obs,
  size = n_trials,
  prob = discrete_post$prob
)
discrete_post$product <- discrete_post$prior * discrete_post$likelihood
marginal_lik <- sum(discrete_post$product)
discrete_post$posterior <- discrete_post$product / marginal_lik

knitr::kable(discrete_post, digits = 4)
```

The marginal likelihood is `r round(marginal_lik, 4)`
(with a uniform prior over eleven values,
the average of the likelihood column),
and the posterior probabilities sum to `r sum(discrete_post$posterior)`.
@fig-discrete-prior compares the prior with the posterior.

```{r}
#| label: fig-discrete-prior
#| fig-cap: "Prior and posterior probabilities on the grid of values of the success probability, after 8 successes in 10 trials."
#| fig-alt: !expr paste0(
#|   "Two bar charts side by side, each with the grid values 0 to 1 on the horizontal axis ",
#|   "and probability on the vertical axis. ",
#|   "The prior panel has eleven bars of equal height, ",
#|   round(1 / nrow(discrete_post), 3), ". ",
#|   "The posterior panel is hump-shaped, ",
#|   "it is tallest at ",
#|   discrete_post$prob[which.max(discrete_post$posterior)],
#|   " with probability ",
#|   round(max(discrete_post$posterior), 3),
#|   ", and the bars at 0 and 1 are zero or nearly zero."
#|   )
discrete_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    prob = discrete_post$prob,
    distribution = "prior",
    probability = discrete_post$prior
  ),
  data.frame(
    prob = discrete_post$prob,
    distribution = "posterior",
    probability = discrete_post$posterior
  )
)
discrete_long$distribution <- factor(
  discrete_long$distribution,
  levels = c("prior", "posterior")
)

ggplot2::ggplot(discrete_long, ggplot2::aes(prob, probability)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.06) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~distribution) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "success probability", y = "probability")
```

{{< slidebreak >}}

To get an interval, accumulate the posterior probabilities
from the bottom of the grid.
For each grid value $\prob_j$,
the upper-tail probability $\Pr(\prob > \prob_j \mid x = 8)$
is one minus the cumulative probability up to and including $\prob_j$.

```{r}
#| label: discrete-prior-tail
#| code-fold: false
discrete_post$cum_posterior <- cumsum(discrete_post$posterior)
discrete_post$upper_tail <- 1 - discrete_post$cum_posterior

lower_bound <- max(discrete_post$prob[discrete_post$upper_tail >= 0.95])
tail_at_bound <- discrete_post$upper_tail[discrete_post$prob == lower_bound]

knitr::kable(
  discrete_post[, c("prob", "posterior", "cum_posterior", "upper_tail")],
  digits = 4
)
```

The largest grid value whose upper-tail probability is still at least 0.95
is $\prob =$ `r lower_bound`.
So $\Pr(\prob > `r lower_bound` \mid x = 8) =$ `r round(tail_at_bound, 4)`,
and the one-sided 95% [credible interval](#def-credible-interval)
for $\prob$ is $(`r lower_bound`, 1]$:
given 8 successes in 10 trials and this prior,
the probability that $\prob$ exceeds `r lower_bound` is at least 0.95.

Unlike a continuous posterior,
a discrete posterior can rarely reach a probability of exactly 0.95,
because its probability comes in lumps.
@def-credible-interval asks for probability exactly $1 - \siglevel$;
on a grid we ask for probability *at least* $1 - \siglevel$,
and take the largest lower endpoint that achieves it.
That makes the interval conservative:
here its posterior probability is `r round(tail_at_bound, 4)`, not 0.95.
:::
